summary:
Tether is an offline-first crew health console for deep-space missions. On a Mars transit, a reply from Earth can take 21 to 59 minutes, and communication can drop entirely, so acute events and slow health drift cannot wait for ground control. Tether runs on the spacecraft: it learns each astronaut's own 14-day baseline, flags deviations with an explainable "Why?" view, and classifies every alert by comparing time-to-harm with the Earth round-trip (ACT_NOW, ACT_THEN_REPORT, CAN_WAIT_FOR_EARTH). It produces action cards and adapts the 24-hour schedule immediately, while a delayed store-and-forward Earth link keeps ground teams informed for monitoring only. Behavioral wellbeing indicators (daily check-in, 60-second reaction test) are read against the person's own baseline, and private journal text never leaves the device. Earth stays informed; the crew stays in control.

details:
Detailed Project Description

What it does. Tether monitors crew health signals (heart rate, SpO2, HRV, sleep, hydration, cabin CO2, radiation, mood check-ins) and turns them into decisions that can be made without waiting for Earth.

How it works. A seven-stage pipeline (ingest, buffer, baseline, modules, detection, decision, persist) runs in a Web Worker in pure TypeScript. Detection has four layers: L1 absolute safety limits, L2 personal deviation against a 14-day rolling median/MAD baseline in 6-hour circadian bins, L3 multi-day trends (CUSUM, Theil-Sen), and L4 inference of seven states (fatigue, stress, dehydration, sleep debt, radiation event, cardio strain, mood decline) with driver attribution. A 48-hour drift guard freezes the baseline during active warnings. A delay-aware triage compares each alert's time-to-harm with 2 x one-way delay + ground processing and classifies it as ACT_NOW, ACT_THEN_REPORT or CAN_WAIT_FOR_EARTH. The planner then produces action cards and adjusts the 24-hour schedule (for example, shelter blocks during a solar particle event). Telemetry is batched every 15 simulated minutes into a delayed "Ground Mirror" with light-time delay, 64 kbps serialization and blackout queuing; journal and check-in notes are stripped before downlink.

Benefits and goals. Faster, explainable onboard decision support for crews that cannot rely on real-time ground support; a continuous but non-blocking Earth view for flight teams.

Validation (synthetic). 8 mission scenarios, 20 held-out seeds, 8,320 crew-days: 0.025 false WARNING+ alerts per nominal crew-day, 95.3% strong-event recall, 15 simulated minutes P90 detection of solar particle events with 100% ACT_NOW triage, and a -1.5% gap between tuning and held-out seeds.

Limitations. All telemetry is synthetic; simulator and detector were written by the same team (circularity risk); not a medical device and no diagnostic claim; bone loss is an indicative estimate; most thresholds are labeled DEMO_PARAMETER.

Tools. TypeScript (strict), React 19, Vite, Tailwind, Zustand, Zod, Dexie (IndexedDB), Web Workers, Vitest (52 test files / 317 tests), PWA service worker. Deployed as a static site.
